title: SSi could-occupy codex: position classes of a single sentence (C1-C24)
purpose: The definitions a model (Haiku family) uses to say which conversational POSITION CLASSES a course's known-side sentence could fill if a turn were built around it. Tom 2026-10-07 (r-2026-10-07-never-use-regex-to-classify-language). Could-occupy, never attestation: a seed has no turn around it. The C-ids and their shape-position mapping are pinned to tools/frame-layer/could-occupy.cjs; C0 'any turn' is a word count and is not in this codex.
task: You classify sentences from a language course (the KNOWN side of seed sentences) by the conversational move each sentence could make if someone said it in a conversation
request: For EACH numbered sentence, give the class ids it belongs to, per the codex. Never output O: this codex has no openers.
example: Example: 5: yes/no question; asks permission 'can I' => C2 C24
general_rules: A class is a property of the sentence ITSELF, read off its own words: the move it would make if said to someone. Be CONSERVATIVE: fire a class only on evidence in the sentence, never because it could fit 'with enough imagination'. A wrongly-tagged sentence poisons a filler pool; an untagged one is an honest hole.
Judge the move and the meaning, never the presence of a word: 'I don't understand why she left' is not a repair (C5); 'thinking about how to answer' is not a hedge (C7).

Multi-label: a sentence can fire several classes ('Can I ask you something before you leave?' fires C2 and C24). Many sentences fire only C6, and one- or two-word fragments ('Woman.', 'An idea.', 'Badly.') usually fire nothing.

Questions are recognised by grammar and the question mark; a statement with a question mark is still a question. A question is never C6. EVERY yes/no question fires C24, also when it fires C1, C2 or C3 ('Can I have something to drink please?' fires C2 AND C24).
The sentence is the known side of a course and may be in a language other than English; apply the same meanings.
When unsure whether a borderline case fires, follow the class's boundary rules; if they do not settle it, do not fire.
output: One line per sentence: '<number>: <tokens>' where tokens are class ids, or '-' when there is nothing. Example: '12: C2 C24'.

frames.name: availability question
frames.shape: is there | have you got | do you have | do you sell [NP] ?
frames.definition: A QUESTION asking whether something is available, exists nearby or is held: is there / are there, have you got, do you have, got any, do you sell, do you know if there is.
positives: Is there a bank near here?
Do you have any snacks?
Have you got a room for tonight?
Are there any trains after midnight?
Do you sell stamps?

near_misses.text: There is a bank near here.
Do you have to go now?
Do you have time to talk?
near_misses.why: asks the other's time as a request, not availability of a thing or place

near_misses.text: Is there anything you want to tell me?

near_misses.why: a personal question about family, not availability of a thing, service or place

boundary: Availability of a thing, service or place; 'is that ...?' identification questions do not fire.

frames.name: possibility / permission question
frames.shape: can I | could I | may I | is it possible | do you mind if ... ?
frames.definition: A QUESTION asking permission for the SPEAKER (or speaker's group) to do something, or whether something is possible: can I, could I, may I, can we, could we, is it possible to, would it be OK, am I allowed to, do you mind if I, is it alright if.
positives: Can I ask you something before you leave?
Could I pay by card?
Is it possible to change my ticket?
Do you mind if I sit here?
May we come in?

near_misses.why: speculation, not permission or practical possibility

near_misses.text: Can I really be so stupid?
Is it possible that he lied?
near_misses.why: asks about likelihood of a fact, not a possibility to act

boundary: The action asked about is the speaker's own (I/we) or an arrangement ('is it possible to...').

frames.name: request of the other
frames.shape: can you | could you | would you (mind) [VP] ? | please [VP] | don't [VP]
frames.definition: The speaker asks or tells the OTHER to do (or not do) something as a request: can you / could you / would you / will you ... ?, would you mind ...?, a sentence opening with 'please' + verb, or a sentence opening with a negative command 'don't ...'.
positives: Could you say that again more slowly?
Can you tell me how far it is into town?
Would you mind closing the window?
Please wait here.
Don't tell anyone.

near_misses.why: asks about ability, not a request

near_misses.text: You could try the other shop.

boundary: Ability questions ('can you swim?') and offers ('would you like...?') do not fire.
'Do you want to [VP]?' fires C3 only when it invites the other to do something with the speaker (and then also C10).

frames.name: wh-question / elicitation
frames.shape: what | where | when | who | why | how | which ... ?
frames.definition: A DIRECT question built on a question word (what, where, when, who, whose, why, how, which, how much/many/long/far), eliciting content rather than yes/no.
positives: Why are you learning her name?
Where are you from?
How far is it into town?
What do you do?
Which one do you want?

near_misses.text: Do you know where the station is?
near_misses.why: a polar question with an embedded wh-clause (C24)

near_misses.text: When I was young, I lived in Spain.
Can you tell me what time it is?
near_misses.why: a request with an embedded question (C3, C24)

boundary: The question word opens the main question; embedded wh-clauses in a polar question do not fire C4.

frames.name: repair initiation
frames.shape: say that again | I didn't catch | I don't understand | what do you mean
frames.definition: The speaker signals NOT UNDERSTANDING or not hearing what was just said and seeks repetition or clarification: could you say that again, I didn't (quite) catch that, I don't understand (you), what do you mean, more slowly please, can you repeat that.
positives: Could you say that again a little more slowly?
I'm sorry, I didn't catch your name.
I don't understand what you mean.
What do you mean by that?
Can you speak more slowly, please?

near_misses.text: I don't understand why she left.
near_misses.why: puzzlement about the world, not about what was just said

near_misses.text: I said it again and again.

boundary: Must concern the interlocutor's immediately preceding words.

frames.name: plain answer / report
frames.shape: [DECLARATIVE CLAUSE]
frames.definition: A full DECLARATIVE statement (subject + verb, at least three words) that tells or reports something and could answer a question: not a question, not a command or request. True of most statements; it is a generic class.
positives: It's on the other side of that yellow line.
I'm from Manchester.
We've only got drinks.
I started to think about it carefully last month.
She told me she has driven that car.
boundary: Imperatives ('Make sure you...', 'Remember to...') are not C6, and nor is advice addressed to the other ('you need to do it before you go' is C12 only).
A stand-alone 'because' clause that answers a why-question ('Because I want to meet people.') IS C6.
Exclamations that are full clauses ('That's wonderful!') do fire C6.

frames.name: hedged answer: roughly, and it depends
frames.shape: maybe | probably | I think | it depends | about [QUANTITY] ...
frames.definition: A STATEMENT (not a question) whose claim is HEDGED by the speaker: maybe, perhaps, probably, possibly, might, I think / I suppose / I'm not sure (as hedges on the claim), it depends, sort of, kind of, more or less, roughly, or 'about/around' in front of a quantity ('about a week', 'around ten').
positives: I've been learning for about a week.
Maybe three or four miles.
I'm not sure if I can remember the whole sentence.
It probably depends on the weather.
I think she's coming tomorrow.

near_misses.text: I started to think about it carefully last month.
near_misses.why: 'about' as a bare preposition, 'think' as a real verb of thinking

near_misses.text: I think about you every day.
near_misses.why: 'think about' = consider, no hedge on a claim

boundary: 'about/around' hedge only before a quantity, number or time.
'I think' hedges only when it introduces an opinion or uncertain claim.

frames.name: can't comply, with a reason
frames.shape: I can't [VP] because | but | I've got to ...
frames.definition: A STATEMENT in which the speaker (or speaker's side) says they CANNOT or WILL NOT do something AND gives a reason in the same sentence: can't / cannot / couldn't / won't / don't want to / not able to + because / but / so / since / as / I've got to / I have to.
positives: I'm sorry but I can't talk at the moment, I need to go home.
I can't come tomorrow because I'm working.
I won't be there, I've got to see the doctor.
I couldn't call you as my phone was dead.
We can't stay long, we have to catch the train.

near_misses.text: I can't wait to see you.

near_misses.why: an exclamation of surprise, no compliance at stake

near_misses.text: I didn't go because it rained.
near_misses.why: a past report of not going, no can't/won't

boundary: Both parts are required: inability/refusal AND a reason.

frames.name: decline / counter with an account
frames.shape: [CLAUSE] but | although | actually | I don't think ...
frames.definition: A STATEMENT of at least five words that pushes back, disagrees, qualifies or declines with an account: contrastive but / although / even though / actually / on the other hand, or a disagreeing 'I don't think...' / 'I'm not sure that...'.
positives: I'm from Manchester, but I live in London now.
I teach English, but not in a school.
Actually, I'd rather stay at home tonight.
I don't think that's a good idea.
It's cheap, although it's a long way from the centre.

near_misses.text: With milk but with no sugar.
near_misses.why: a fragment, under five words of clause

near_misses.text: I think it's a good idea.

boundary: Needs a contrast or disagreement and at least five words.

frames.name: proposal
frames.shape: shall we | let's | why don't we | how about | we could | do you want to ...
frames.definition: The speaker PROPOSES a joint or suggested course of action: shall we, let's, why don't we, how about (+ action), we could, we should, do you want to / would you like to (invitation to do something).
positives: Shall we meet at eight?
But let's talk on Saturday.
Why don't we take the bus?
How about a coffee after work?
Would you like to come with us?

near_misses.why: 'let me' asks room for the speaker, not a joint plan
an offer of a thing, not of a joint action

boundary: Offers of things ('would you like some tea?') do not fire; invitations to an activity do.

frames.name: acceptance / uptake
frames.shape: yes | of course | great | perfect | no problem ...
frames.definition: The sentence OPENS with an acceptance, polar response or evaluative uptake that responds to someone: yes, no, of course, certainly, absolutely, great, perfect, lovely, excellent, no problem, that's fine, good idea, exactly, how interesting.
positives: Yes, please.
Of course, no problem at all.
Great, I'll see you there.
No, I'm busy tomorrow.
Perfect, that's exactly what I wanted.

near_misses.why: assessment inside a report, not opening uptake

near_misses.text: Exactly two hours later, he left.
Of course he knows, he's his father.
near_misses.why: emphasis inside a statement, not uptake of a prior move

boundary: Must open the sentence and respond to a prior move.

frames.name: instruction / advice
frames.shape: [IMPERATIVE] | you need to | you should | make sure | remember to ...
frames.definition: A STATEMENT or IMPERATIVE addressed TO THE OTHER telling them what to do: an imperative ('Take two tablets', 'Turn left'), 'you need to / have to / ought to / should / must / you'll need to', or opening 'make sure', 'remember to', 'don't forget'.
positives: You should ask yourself why it's not working.
Take two tablets after breakfast.
Make sure you lock the door.
You'll need to bring your passport.
Don't forget to call your mother.

near_misses.text: I'm going to try to explain what I mean.
They want to make sure it works.
I need to go home now.
And I want you to speak Norwegian with me tomorrow.
near_misses.why: states the speaker's wish; not an instruction or advice form

boundary: Must carry a second-person addressee (explicit 'you' or an imperative).

frames.name: read-back / receipt
frames.shape: got it | understood | that's right ...
frames.definition: The speaker MARKS RECEIPT of an instruction or information: got it, understood, noted, that's right, exactly right, word perfect.
positives: Got it.
Understood, Monday at nine.
That's right.
Noted, thank you.
Exactly right, two after each meal.

near_misses.text: That's right next to the bank.

boundary: Only the speaker's own receipt formula.

frames.name: thanks / downgrade
frames.shape: thank you | thanks ...
frames.definition: The speaker THANKS the other: thank you, thanks, much obliged, I appreciate it, that's very kind of you.
positives: Thank you very much.
Thanks for your help.
I'm very well, thank you.
I really appreciate it.
That's very kind of you.

near_misses.text: Thanks to you, I missed the bus.

boundary: The speaker's own thanks only.

frames.name: compliment / positive assessment of the other
frames.shape: you're (very|so) [ADJ] | well done | you look [ADJ] ...
frames.definition: The speaker PRAISES or POSITIVELY ASSESSES THE OTHER person or what they did: you're very kind / so clever, that's very kind of you, you look great, well done, you've done really well, your French is very good.
positives: You're very kind.
Well done, that's further than yesterday.
You look lovely today.
Your Spanish is really good.
You've done a great job.

near_misses.why: about the world, not the other

boundary: The praise must be aimed at the addressee or their work.

frames.name: self-downgrade
frames.shape: I'm not very good | I don't speak it very well | I'm still learning ...
frames.definition: The speaker PLAYS DOWN their own skill or standing: I'm not very good (at it), I'm only a beginner, I don't speak it very well, I'm still learning, I'm no good at, my Spanish isn't very good.
positives: I'm not very good at maths.
I don't speak it very well yet.
I'm still learning, sorry.
My Welsh isn't very good.
I don't know how to say enough different words yet.

near_misses.text: He's not very good at football.
I'm still waiting for the bus.

near_misses.why: a plain report of learning, no downgrade

near_misses.text: I speak a little Dutch now.

boundary: About the speaker's own ability or standing, as modesty.

frames.name: trouble declaration
frames.shape: I've got a bad [N] | I'm (ill|worried) | it hurts | there's a problem ...
frames.definition: The SPEAKER declares their own trouble, pain, illness, worry or a problem they have: I've got a bad back, I'm not feeling well, I'm worried, it hurts, my head hurts, I can't sleep, there's a problem with my room.
positives: I've got a terrible headache.
I'm not feeling very well.
It hurts when I cough.
There's a problem with my room.
I can't sleep at night.

near_misses.text: She was very kind when she saw me feeling nervous.
near_misses.why: narrative description, not the speaker declaring a current trouble

near_misses.text: I was worried you wouldn't come.

boundary: The trouble is the speaker's own and named, in the present.

frames.name: not-knowing, held
frames.shape: I don't know | I've no idea | I'm not sure | I can't remember ...
frames.definition: The speaker STATES THEY DO NOT KNOW or cannot remember something: I don't know, I've no idea, I have no idea, I'm not sure, I can't remember, nobody knows.
positives: I don't know how to say that.
I've no idea where he is.
I'm not sure if I can remember the whole sentence.
I can't remember her name.
Nobody knows why.

near_misses.text: I don't know him very well.
near_misses.why: acquaintance with a person, not a missing piece of information

boundary: Lack of information or memory, said by the speaker.
'I'm not sure if/whether ...' fires C18 (and C7).

frames.name: claim / generalisation
frames.shape: always | never | everyone | people ... | it's important | in general
frames.definition: A STATEMENT making a general claim beyond one event: with always, never (as a generalisation), everyone, everybody, people (in general), usually, generally, in general, it's important to, the thing is.
positives: People always say that.
It's important to drink water.
Everyone needs a holiday.
I never eat meat.
Generally, the trains are on time.

near_misses.why: a negative pronoun in a plain report

near_misses.text: Everyone came to the party last night.

near_misses.why: a personal experience report, not a general claim

near_misses.text: The people next door are nice.

boundary: A habit or truth stated as general; single past events do not fire.

frames.name: anecdote opener
frames.shape: when I was [X] | the other day | last week | years ago | I remember ...
frames.definition: A STATEMENT that opens or sets up a personal past narrative with a dated or framed past: when I was young, the other day, last week/night/year, years ago, I remember (when).
positives: When I was a child, I lived by the sea.
The other day I saw your brother.
Last week we went to Cardiff.
Years ago, this was a farm.
I remember the first time I came here.

near_misses.text: Last time we talked, you were ill.
near_misses.why: refers to a previous conversation, not a narrative
a general present, not a past narrative

boundary: Needs a framed past that a story could follow.

frames.name: greeting / ritual open or close
frames.shape: hello | good morning | goodbye | see you ...
frames.definition: The speaker ritually opens or closes an encounter: hello, hi, good morning/afternoon/evening, welcome, pleased/nice to meet you, goodbye, bye, good night, see you later/tomorrow.
positives: Good morning.
See you tomorrow.
Nice to meet you.
Goodbye, and thank you.
Hello, how are you?

near_misses.text: Did you have a good morning?
I said goodbye to my family.

near_misses.why: arranges a meeting at a place; not a parting formula

near_misses.text: It's a good evening for a walk.

boundary: The speaker's own greeting or farewell.

frames.name: reckoning
frames.shape: that's [AMOUNT OF MONEY] ( altogether )
frames.definition: The speaker STATES AN AMOUNT OF MONEY OWED or a total price: that's eight pounds forty, that'll be five euros, it comes to twelve pounds.
positives: That's eight pound forty altogether.
That'll be five euros.
It comes to twelve pounds.
That's ten dollars, please.
Altogether that's twenty pounds.
boundary: A sum the hearer owes or a transaction total.

frames.name: explicit park
frames.shape: let's leave it | we'll talk about it later | another time ...
frames.definition: The speaker explicitly PUTS A TOPIC OR TASK ASIDE for later: let's leave it (there), let's come back to that, we'll talk about it later / another time, another time, let's park that.
positives: Let's leave it for now.
We'll talk about it another time.
Let's come back to that later.
Maybe another time.
We can discuss it tomorrow.
boundary: A topic or task is deferred, explicitly.

frames.name: polar question
frames.shape: [AUX] [SUBJ] ... ?
frames.definition: A YES/NO question (including questions with an embedded wh-clause, tag questions and declarative questions with a question mark), i.e. any question that is NOT a direct wh-question.
positives: Do you speak Spanish all day?
Is this seat taken?
Can you tell me how far it is into town?
You're French?
Did you have a long day?

near_misses.text: He asked whether I was tired.

boundary: C24 and C4 never both fire on the same single question; a sentence with two questions may fire both.
